name: Mexenone

lead: Mexenone (benzophenone-10) is a UV-absorbing sunscreen filter related to oxybenzone. The appearance payoff is less cumulative sun damage, which is what drives wrinkling, rough texture and uneven tone over the years.

It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure, so less reaches skin cells. Most of what has been published on it comes from dermatology clinics: patch-test series from the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly listed it among the most frequent sunscreen allergens.

paras: It was formulated into sunscreens as one of several filters. Protection is cumulative, so any visible difference in wrinkles and tone shows up over years of regular sun protection rather than weeks. It is not a common ingredient in current routines.

Contact allergy and photoallergy are its main documented problem. Patch-test series found roughly 5 to 7.5% of tested patients reacting to sunscreens overall, with mexenone among the leading culprits. People with a history of reacting to oxybenzone or other benzophenones are the ones most likely to be affected. Its current regulatory status was not documented.

angle.text: Mexenone is an older sunscreen filter that absorbs UV so less sun damage reaches your skin, which slows sun-driven wrinkling and uneven tone over the years. It is known more from dermatology allergy clinics than from current skincare routines.

lead: Mexenone (benzophenone-10, trade name Uvistat) is a benzophenone-derived sunscreening agent with the chemical name (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(4-methylphenyl)methanone (C15H14O3) [1]. It is chemically related to oxybenzone (benzophenone-3) [2]. Like other UV filters, its role in appearance is skin protection: absorbing ultraviolet light so that skin burns, tans and photoages less, which keeps tone and texture looking younger over time.

In the dermatology literature it is best documented as a contact and photocontact allergen. Patch-test series from clinics in the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly reported mexenone as one of the most frequent sunscreen sensitisers [3][4], and a 2023 Singapore photopatch series still listed it among the commonest relevant reactions [5]. A 1975 comparison of sunscreen preparations found it the least effective individually against sunburn wavelengths among the agents tested, with a para-aminobenzoic acid mixture performing best [6]. Newer research uses the molecule outside sun protection: a 2024 mouse study identified it as a vascular-permeability blocker in a lipopolysaccharide sepsis model [7].

paras: Mexenone has a molar mass of about 242 g/mol and is one of the numbered benzophenone sunscreen agents.[1] It is one of several benzophenone UV filters alongside oxybenzone.[1][2]

In a 1987 report from a UK contact dermatitis clinic, 15 of 280 patients (5%) tested with sunscreens reacted, and mexenone was the most frequent allergen (six patients).[3] A 1993 study of 214 patients with photosensitivity disorders or polymorphic light eruption, and controls, found 16 (7.5%) reacting to at least one sunscreen; benzophenones (mexenone and oxybenzone) accounted for 8 of 27 positive patch tests.[4] A 1980 case report described mexenone allergy that presented as a flare of light sensitivity,[8] and a 1991 paper examined contact and photocontact allergy to oxybenzone and mexenone.[2]
Studies of photopatch testing set the UV-A dose needed to provoke responses in people already sensitised to agents including mexenone, oxybenzone and isopropyl dibenzoylmethane.[9]

The 1975 British Journal of Dermatology study tested chemical light-screening agents on 104 non-photosensitive volunteers and 78 people with photodermatoses. The most effective preparation against short UV (below 320 nm) was a mixture of 5 percent para-aminobenzoic acid and 2.5 percent of an amyl ester, and mexenone was least effective individually; protection fell after showering but not after exercise [6].

In a photopatch dose study, four patients who had reacted before to mexenone, isopropyl dibenzoylmethane and oxybenzone were re-exposed at incremental UV-A doses; positive responses appeared at about 1.0 J/cm2 for mexenone and isopropyl dibenzoylmethane and 0.7 J/cm2 for oxybenzone, and the authors concluded that very high UV-A doses were unnecessary and that 5 J/cm2 should become the standard [9]. In a ten-year Singapore review of 90 patients photopatch tested from 2012 to 2021, relevant reactions were commonest to oxybenzone (9.5 percent) and mexenone (3.6 percent) [5].

Human studies of mexenone are patch-test and photopatch-test series in dermatology clinics rather than trials of sun protection. These report mexenone as a leading cause of sunscreen allergy in the clinics studied, with sensitisation in roughly 5 to 7.5% of patients tested with sunscreen series in the 1987 and 1993 reports.[3][4] A 2006 Colombian series of photoallergic contact dermatitis also listed sunscreen causes among its findings.[10]
A 1975 study of 182 volunteers compared sunscreen preparations for burn protection, and a 2023 Singapore review of 90 photopatch-tested patients reported mexenone reactions in 3.6 percent [6][5].
A 1975 paper surveyed chemical light-screening agents of the time.[6] Mexenone is not a common topic in appearance forums.
